This page collects general advice on how to write [proofs](notation.qmd#def-proof) and [derivations](notation.qmd#def-derivation).
The goal of a proof is not just to convince yourself that a [result](notation.qmd#def-theorem) is true;
it is to convince a *reader*,
and to show them *why* it is true.
Each principle on this page serves that goal.
The symbols for [logical entailment](notation.qmd#def-logical-entailment) are listed under
[Proofs](notation.qmd#proofs) on the Notation page.

## Don't skip steps {#sec-dont-skip-steps}

Show every step of the derivation.
Each line should follow from the previous line by a single, identifiable move:

- applying a definition,
- substituting a known result, or
- performing one algebraic operation.

When you skip steps,
you force the reader to reconstruct your reasoning,
which is exactly the work the proof was supposed to do *for* them.
A step that feels "obvious" while you are writing it
is often the step a reader gets stuck on.
Phrases like "it can be shown that" or "clearly"
usually mark a skipped step;
show the step instead.

## Annotate each step {#sec-annotate-each-step}

For each step,
note the definition, [theorem](notation.qmd#def-theorem), or algebraic rule that justifies it.
A brief annotation to the right of the line is usually enough.
Annotations make the proof checkable,
and they teach the reader which tool to reach for in similar situations.

For example,
here is a derivation that the
[hat matrix](linear-algebra.qmd#def-hat-matrix)
$\matr{H} = \mX(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}$
is [idempotent](linear-algebra.qmd#def-idempotent-matrix), $\matr{H}^2 = \matr{H}$,
with each step annotated:

$$
\ba
\matr{H}^2
&= \matr{H}\matr{H}
&& \text{(definition of a matrix power)}
\\
&= \mX(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}\,\mX(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}
&& \text{(definition of } \matr{H} \text{)}
\\
&= \mX(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}(\tp{\mX}\mX)(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}
&& \text{(regroup; matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \mX\,\matr{I}_p\,(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}
&& \text{(a matrix inverse times the matrix is } \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \mX(\tp{\mX}\mX)^{-1}\tp{\mX}
&& \text{(the identity matrix changes nothing)}
\\
&= \matr{H}
&& \text{(definition of } \matr{H} \text{)}
\ea
$$

The [Linear Algebra](linear-algebra.qmd#thm-hat-matrix) page
uses this derivation to show that $\matr{H}$ is a
[projection matrix](linear-algebra.qmd#def-projection-matrix).
The probability notes derive the variance identity
$\Var{X} = \E{X^2} - \sqf{\E{X}}$
[in the same annotated style](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#thm-variance).

## Direct proof {#sec-direct-proof}

:::{#def-direct-proof}
#### Direct proof

A **direct proof** of a proposition $Q$
starts from the assumptions that $Q$ is stated under, if any,
and reaches $Q$ through a chain of steps,
each of which applies a definition,
a previously proved result,
or one rule of logic or algebra
to the assumptions or to earlier steps.
A direct proof never assumes that $Q$ is false;
compare [proof by contradiction](notation.qmd#def-proof-by-contradiction),
which does.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-direct-proof}
#### The square of an odd integer is odd

Claim: if $n$ is an [odd](notation.qmd#def-even-odd) integer,
then $n^2$ is odd.

Since $n$ is odd,
there is an integer $k$ with $n = 2k + 1$.
Then

$$
\ba
n^2
&= (2k + 1)^2
&& \text{(substitute } n = 2k + 1 \text{)}
\\&= (2k)^2 + 2 \cd 2k \cd 1 + 1^2
&& \text{(square of a sum)}
\\&= 4k^2 + 4k + 1
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\\&= 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\ea
$$

and $2k^2 + 2k$ is an integer,
because sums and products of integers are integers.
So $n^2 = 2 \cd (\text{an integer}) + 1$, which is the definition of odd.
For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
n &= 7 \\
&= 2 \cd 3 + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
n^2 &= 49 \\
&= 2 \cd 24 + 1,
\end{aligned}
$$

and $2 \cd 3^2 + 2 \cd 3 = 24$.

The notation page's proof that
[the sum of two even integers is even](notation.qmd#exm-proof)
is also a direct proof.

:::

## Follow the golden rule {#sec-golden-rule}

In general,
follow the golden rule:
treat your readers the way you want to be treated as a reader.

When you read someone else's proof,
you want to be able to follow every step without guessing,
to know which result is being used at each line,
and to never be left wondering where a quantity came from.
Write your own proofs to meet that same standard.

## Proof by induction {#sec-proof-by-induction}

Many proofs in these notes show that a statement holds
for every [natural number](notation.qmd#def-natural-numbers) $n$,
or for every integer $n$ from some starting value on.
Checking the statement one $n$ at a time would never finish;
induction proves it for all of them with two arguments.

## Formal logic {#sec-formal-logic}

:::{#def-propositional-logic}
#### Propositional logic

**Propositional logic** is the study of
[logical entailment](notation.qmd#def-logical-entailment)
among [propositions](notation.qmd#def-proposition)
built from basic propositions $P, Q, R, \ldots$
using only the [logical connectives](notation.qmd#def-logical-connective).
Whether such propositions entail one another
depends only on the truth values of the basic propositions,
not on what the basic propositions say.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-propositional-logic}
#### $P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$ entail $Q$

Suppose $P$ is true and $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true.
If $Q$ were false,
then $P \Rightarrow Q$ would have a true $P$ and a false $Q$,
so $P \Rightarrow Q$ would be false,
which contradicts the assumption.
So $Q$ is true.
This holds whatever $P$ and $Q$ say,
so $P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$ logically entail $Q$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-first-order-logic}
#### First-order logic

**First-order logic** extends propositional logic (@def-propositional-logic)
by also allowing:

- variables $x, y, \ldots$ that stand for elements of a set;
- [predicates](notation.qmd#def-predicate) of one or more of those variables,
  such as $P(x)$ or $x < y$;
- [functions](sets-functions.qmd#def-function) of them, such as $x + y$;
- equality between them;
- [quantifiers](notation.qmd#def-quantifier) $\forall$ and $\exists$ over them.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-first-order-logic}
#### From "for all" to one element

Let $P(x)$ be a predicate about the elements of a set $S$,
and let $a \in S$.
The propositions $\forall x \in S, P(x)$ and $a \in S$
logically entail $P(a)$:
if $P(x)$ is true for every element $x$ of $S$,
then it is true for the element $a$.
For example,
$\forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, x^2 \ge 0$ entails $3^2 \ge 0$.
Propositional logic alone cannot express this entailment,
because it has no way to refer to the elements of $S$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-formal-proof}
#### Formal proof

A **formal proof** is a [proof](notation.qmd#def-proof)
written in propositional logic (@def-propositional-logic)
or first-order logic (@def-first-order-logic)
in which each step is an assumption
or follows from earlier steps by one rule
taken from a fixed list of allowed rules,
so that checking the proof needs no understanding of what its propositions mean.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-formal-proof}
#### A three-step formal proof

Suppose the allowed rules include
"from $P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$, conclude $Q$".
Then this is a formal proof of $Q$ from the assumptions $P$ and $P \Rightarrow Q$:

1. $P$ (assumption)
2. $P \Rightarrow Q$ (assumption)
3. $Q$ (from steps 1 and 2, by the rule above)

:::
